title: Signs of progress
hook: the one making progress blames no one, praises no one, and claims to know nothing (Enchiridion 48)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the cold water, spat out, and told to no one. Your line was in secret. Did you keep one discipline quiet all day? Day three hundred eighty-three.

How would you know if any of this is working? Progress bars are easy when it's a language or a marathon. Words learned, miles run. But a calmer mind doesn't come with a counter. Epictetus' students wanted to know the same thing: am I actually getting anywhere? Section forty-eight answers them with a checklist. It isn't the checklist anyone expects. There's nothing on it about feeling peaceful, or knowing more. It's mostly about what you stop doing. Today: signs of progress.
screen: `HOW WOULD YOU KNOW IT'S WORKING?` → `A CALM MIND HAS NO COUNTER.` → `SIGNS OF PROGRESS.`

segments.voice: First, two positions. The ordinary person, Epictetus says, expects help or harm to come from outside. The person on this path expects help or harm to come from inside, from their own judgments. Second, the checklist. The one making progress blames no one. Praises no one. Finds fault with no one. Accuses no one. Says nothing about themselves as if they were somebody, or knew something. When they're blocked, they look to themselves. When they're praised, they laugh quietly to themselves at the one praising. When they're criticized, they don't defend themselves. Third, the patient. Such a person, he says, goes about like someone recovering from an illness, careful not to disturb something that's healing before it has set firm. That's a gentle picture. Progress here isn't a trophy. It's a mending bone, and you walk carefully on it. Fourth, the word. The Stoics called this prokopē, progress, and the one making it a prokoptōn. Many Stoics said the perfectly wise person was so rare that perhaps none had ever lived. Everyone else, Epictetus included, was somewhere on the road. That's why the checklist matters. You'll never be told you've arrived. But you can notice, on an ordinary Tuesday, that you didn't blame anyone for the traffic, didn't need the compliment, didn't defend yourself against the remark. Those are the signs. Small, quiet, and real. Notice which sign leads the list. Not courage, not wisdom. Blame no one.
screen: `HELP AND HARM COME FROM INSIDE.` · `BLAMES NO ONE, PRAISES NO ONE.` · `LIKE SOMEONE RECOVERING, CAREFUL.` · `PROKOPĒ: SOMEWHERE ON THE ROAD.` · then, large: `BLAME NO ONE.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Run Epictetus' checklist slowly, as a mirror, not a test. Blames no one. Praises no one, finds fault with no one. Says nothing about being somebody. Laughs a little at praise. Doesn't defend against criticism. Which one is closest to true for you lately? Which is farthest? Pick one sign to watch for in yourself today, and hold it gently, like a bone that's still mending. The bell holds the time.
Prokopē. The Stoic word for progress, and the one making it. Its first sign, in Enchiridion forty-eight: blame no one. Today's word.
Your line: blame no one. Check one sign in yourself today. When something goes wrong, notice the urge to blame, and let it pass. Day three hundred eighty-three.

howItsDone: People practicing Stoicism sometimes review Epictetus' signs of progress, especially blaming no one, as a quiet self-check at the end of the day.

fork.setup: your project fails, partly because of a colleague. what would the one making progress do first?
options: make sure everyone knows whose fault it was.
blame no one, and look to their own part.
say it's fine and praise the colleague.
fork.reveal: the first sign on the list: blames no one. when blocked, the one making progress looks to themselves.

original.note: Greek: progress. The Stoics called the one making it a prokoptōn.

trapdoor: what you thought: progress means feeling better.
what it means: progress shows in what you stop doing: blaming, praising, accusing, talking yourself up.
what a scholar hears: prokopē; Stoics doubted a perfect sage had ever lived, so Epictetus counted himself among the prokoptontes.

notes: Enchiridion 48 paraphrased: the uninstructed expect help or harm from externals, the philosopher from himself; signs of one making progress: censures, praises, blames, accuses no one; says nothing of himself as being anybody or knowing anything; when hindered, blames himself; laughs inwardly at praise; makes no defense against censure; goes about like an invalid, careful not to disturb what is healing. Confirm.

'Many Stoics said the perfectly wise person was so rare that perhaps none had ever lived' (cf. Alexander of Aphrodisias' report comparing the sage to the phoenix; Seneca, Letter 42). Confirm phrasing.
Greek προκοπή and προκόπτων: confirm. No etymology claimed.
